Photograph: Parliament TV/PA Assisted dying Analysis Why did the assisted dying bill fail in the Commons? Rowena Mason Whitehall editor MPs quietly withdrew support when it became clear it was not a priority of Andy Burnham’s government MPs vote against legalising assisted dying in England and Wales Fri 11 Sep 2026 13.54 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.52 EDT Share After two years of impassioned arguments, tearful personal testimonies, noisy protests and ethical dilemmas, the assisted dying bill for England and Wales failed on a knife edge. Campaigners on the pro side largely blame the House of Lords for making it seem an impossible struggle to get the bill through parliament, after blocking it the first time by putting through more than 1,000 amendments so that it ran out of time. The opponents are more inclined to think that they ended up picking so many holes in the legislation that it was bound to fail, as they raised more and more objections on safety grounds. But the truth was that many MPs felt momentum was lost when it became clear it was not a priority of Andy Burnham’s government. Although as Greater Manchester mayor he had said he would probably vote in favour of the initial private member’s bill, in July Burnham said he now thought the bigger issue should be to improve end-of-life support . How did your MP vote on the reintroduced assisted dying bill? Read more It suddenly became very unlikely that the government would throw its weight behind giving the bill its full backing or expending energy on policy development to help it succeed. Burnham’s change of position was a blow to the pro campaigners after Keir Starmer had long given his tacit support to the first bill proposed by Kim Leadbeater, even though it was a conscience vote. In private, many MPs also admit that another factor in losing support for the bill was that backing it did not do Starmer’s administration many favours. The bill caused bitter division among its MPs and diverted attention from the many pressing issues that might be more electorally important to Labour , such as the cost of living and healthcare. As it took up more and more parliamentary bandwidth and media airtime, former chief of staff Morgan McSweeney was among the advisers who thought the legislation was a bad idea. There were also some reservations about the sponsors of the bill hoping to use the Parliament Act to force it through if blocked a second time by the Lords, with a rule that states if the same bill is approved twice by the Commons in two consecutive sessions and opposed by peers, then it can be passed anyway. ‘A tragic day’: campaigners react as MPs say no to legalising assisted dying Read more However, this would have meant it being unchanged from the bill presented last year – which worried some MPs who voted for the bill in principle but wanted to see it amended with further protections against coercion. One of the many with a complicated personal position on the issue was Labour MP David Burton-Sampson, who voted in favour of it progressing to give people individual choice, even though he was personally against assisted dying because of his Christian faith; however, he said he would be uncomfortable with it passing into law without further safeguards. When it became clear that Burnham lacked enthusiasm for the bill, it ultimately gave some of those MPs who supported it in theory – but had misgivings about it in practice – permission to absent themselves from the vote. The quiet withdrawal of support is evident in the numbers: the last time MPs voted, 291 voted against it, versus 314 in favour. This time, 286 voted against, while just 270 were in favour, a fall of 45. Campaigners in favour of assisted dying say it is not the end of the road for their efforts to secure a change in the law – and the public still seems to be in favour of the policy in essence. But MPs are likely to be wary of devoting much more time in this parliament to a debate when the arguments have been rehearsed near exhaustively and opinion in parliament is still so evenly split. https://business-review.eu/tech/it/30-ye.text: 30 years of Microsoft in Romania: A solid foundation for the country to move forward more quickly into AI era Thirty years after Microsoft first arrived in Romania, the company is demonstrating how this gap can become an opportunity, provided AI is adopted responsibly: Romanian businesses can become more productive and innovative; public services can become simpler and more accessible; people can develop the skills they need in the AI economy; and Romania can increase its competitiveness and resilience. “Romania has everything it needs to take full advantage of AI: talented people, a dynamic tech ecosystem and resources for investment. Now it needs to act quickly, because the countries that get a head start will gain the most. For thirty years we have been growing alongside Romania’s tech sector, and we want to remain just as closely involved with it in the age of AI. “We are putting our technology, expertise and people at the service of this ambition, so that AI can bring new opportunities to Romanian companies, make public services more efficient for citizens and help Romania compete with the best-performing countries in Europe,” said Gabriela Popescu, General Manager, Microsoft Romania, Moldova & CIS. “ Microsoft’s 30 years in Romania speak volumes about what the company has brought to this country. They speak just as much about America’s leading role in technology and innovation. Thirty years ago, few would have imagined just how pervasive American technology would become in Romania’s economy and in the everyday lives of Romanians. Today, this legacy is one of the clearest and most successful examples of what the Romanian-American partnership can achieve. “The cloud, artificial intelligence and cyber security open up huge opportunities, and if Romania continues to improve its legal framework and governance, it has every chance of capitalising on them alongside American companies such as Microsoft,” said David Galbraith, Deputy Chief of Mission at the US Embassy in Romania. Four ways in which AI can drive Romania’s progress Read more about Accenture: 76% of consumers are open to working with an AI agent for holiday shopping read more Microsoft has identified four areas where AI can make the greatest difference for Romania and where the company will focus its technology, expertise and partnerships. New opportunities for Romanian businesses. With the help of AI, businesses of all sizes can become more productive, enter new markets and launch new products and services. Microsoft will continue to support the responsible adoption of AI in the private sector, in line with European values and regulations, so that the benefits reach businesses that do not yet use this technology. Simpler and more accessible public services. The secure cloud and AI can make public services simpler, faster and easier to access. Microsoft will continue to support the country’s digital transformation, particularly in public administration, education and healthcare, so that people can feel the difference every time they interact with public institutions. S kills for the AI economy. Engineers are one of Romania’s most valuable assets. Together with universities, partners and institutions, Microsoft will continue to invest in digital skills and the local innovation ecosystem, so that students and professionals are prepared to work alongside AI. A more competitive and resilient country. When deployed on a large scale and protected by robust cybersecurity, AI can boost productivity across the economy and strengthen the country’s resilience, enabling Romania to compete on an equal footing with other European Union member states. Romanian companies leading the way in AI Microsoft’s Work Trend Index 2025 report describes a new type of company, the Frontier Firm: an organisation built around on-demand intelligence, where people and AI agents work together and rethink the way work is done. Among the Romanian companies that have already embarked on this journey are Microsoft clients Regina Maria and Banca Transilvania, as well as partner Druid AI. Their experience demonstrates what large-scale AI adoption entails. “We have a long-standing partnership with Microsoft and are delighted to have had it for so long; we will continue to rely on them for the next 30 years. We wish them every success and believe that, at a time when everyone is talking about AI and digitalisation, it is extremely important to have a reliable partner who can bring you innovations from abroad and, above all, the use cases that exist in the fields of healthcare, public health and the quality of medical services,” said Fady Chreih, CEO of the REGINA MARIA Healthcare Network. “Romania is where Druid AI took root and the market in which we have grown. Microsoft has been our partner from day one, and our shared story began even before Druid. We are grateful for the partnership, for the technology and, above all, for the people at Microsoft,” said Andreea Pleșea, Co-founder and Chief Operating Officer, Druid AI . “Our platform runs on Microsoft Azure and complements Microsoft Copilot with AI agents that are tested and controlled according to clear rules. Thanks to this partnership, AI adoption is moving beyond the pilot project stage to the ‘Frontier Firm’ model described above. The gap is bridged when companies put AI agents to work to deliver concrete business results, with governance rules that management can fully trust. This is what we’re focusing on, together with Microsoft.” Thirty years alongside Romania Since 1996, when it opened its first office in Romania, Microsoft has worked with public institutions, companies, partners and the entire tech ecosystem to support the digitalisation of the Romanian economy and society. Today, Romania is one of Microsoft’s most important talent hubs in the region. Around 2,000 employees work in Bucharest, Iași and Timișoara, and the team continues to grow, with several vacancies currently available. The teams in Romania are responsible for key engineering, development and customer support activities across many other markets. For the sixth year running, Microsoft has been named the most desirable employer in Romania in the Most Desired Employers 2026 survey, conducted by Catalyst Solutions based on nearly 10,900 responses. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/27/us-b.text: A localised ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky went into effect early on Tuesday.The local pause in fighting started at 3 am to allow an aid mission into Oleshky in southern Ukraine later this week.According to her office, Melania Trump led talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine after meeting with UN officials who briefed her on the situation in the town.The aid mission is planned ahead of a new round of US-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine expected next month aimed at ending the war after more than 4½ years of fighting.Up to 2,000 people are stranded in Oleshky with dwindling food and medicine. They are unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, according to the UN.Russian and Ukrainian negotiators as well as the militaries of the two countries confirmed in separate statements that the ceasefire had begun.Announcing last Friday that she had brokered the ceasefire, Melania Trump said civilian officials from both Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and "determine the level of assistance they require"."Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," she said.Newsmax, a right-wing US cable network, has said it had been granted "exclusive television access" to accompany observers entering the city on Thursday.Kyiv struck by wave of Russian strikesMinutes after 3 am, multiple ballistic missile explosions shook Kyiv and air alerts sounded in multiple parts of the country.A Russian strike damaged a major bridge spanning the Dnipro River in Kyiv, the city's mayor said."A strike hit the Southern Bridge. Metro infrastructure on the bridge was also damaged," Mayor Vitaly Klitschko wrote on Telegram, with city officials adding that train services across the bridge had been suspended.Late Monday, the capital also came under attack, when Russian ballistic missiles damaged the grounds of a university in Kyiv, killing one person and leaving 10 injured, city officials said.Moscow's latest pummelling has damaged medical facilities in the capital, Klitschko said, adding that a "blast wave shattered the windows in (an) intensive care unit"."At another medical facility in the same district, windows were also shattered in two wards. Neither patients nor medical staff were wounded," he said on social media.In another attack, "a building in a non-residential area was also hit. According to preliminary reports, there is one fatality near one of the supermarkets in the area," Klitschko said.A strike near a dormitory belonging to one of Kyiv's universities has shattered windows in the building, wounding a 20-year-old woman, Klitschko said.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said "Russian ballistic missiles struck the grounds of a university in Kyiv and the area around it –- effectively the campus, Kyoto Park, the area near a metro station, and residential buildings.""The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby. This was a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure," he said on social media.In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, authorities said attacks late Monday killed two people and injured four.“It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war,” Zelenskyy wrote in an online post shortly afterward.
